wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Kellerberg above Dürnstein: steep dry stone terraces of Gföhl gneiss facing south to south east, sheltered from the westerly winds of the Ice Ages, so patches of loess survive. Its name, from the baroque Kellerschlössl of Dürnstein, dates only from 1787 and gathered several smaller vineyards.
wine.making: Picked by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires of every wine and the ripeness of a Smaragd asks. The codex of the Vinea Wachau forbids any enrichment of the must and allows a Smaragd no hint of oak, and the wine is fermented dry; the house speaks of as little intervention as it can manage in the cellar.
wine.glass: Mango, passion fruit and pineapple over ripe yellow peach and a stony core; dense and broad for a dry Riesling, with high extract, ripe acidity and an alcohol that reads as weight rather than heat, and it lingers.
wine.ageing: Broad from the start, it is at its fullest after eight to ten years; strong vintages last twenty years and beyond.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems closed; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named for the emerald lizard.
The single vineyard; Austrian law asks for the word Ried before a vineyard's name.
The older form on the label, the Kellerberg of Dürnstein, before Ried was required.
The appellation since the 2020 vintage; its single vineyard wines are Grüner Veltliner or Riesling alone.

records.table: On steep gneiss terraces above Dürnstein in the Wachau, F.X. Pichler grows its Riesling Smaragd Ried Kellerberg. Dry yet broad, with mango and ripe peach over stone, it carries the weight of the valley's ripest style, so chill it only lightly.
records.story: A grower from Rohrendorf near Krems, a forebear of the family, moved into the Wachau in the middle of the nineteenth century, the house recounts, and a grandson bought a property at Oberloiben in 1898; the house dates its winery there to 1905. The F.X. of the name, a later grower of the family who studied at the wine school of Krems and worked vintages in Germany and Alsace, set out to show each site at the full ripeness of its grapes. In 1983 the growers of the valley founded the Vinea Wachau, with its codex against enrichment and its three styles of Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, and F.X. Pichler stood with it from the beginning. Two years later a scandal over doctored sweet wines emptied Austria's export markets and brought a strict new wine law. The Riesling Kellerberg of 1990 was, by the house's own reckoning, the wine that carried its name abroad, as the dry Smaragd wines of the Wachau led Austria's recovery. In 2009 the family moved into a new winery at Oberloiben, and the Kellerberg has been a Ried of the Wachau DAC since the 2020 vintage. In the glass it is the measure of how much ripeness a dry Riesling can carry.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Loibenberg
others.note: Warmer and broader, from the hill above Loiben, the direct comparison with the Kellerberg.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Kellerberg
others.note: Grüner Veltliner at full Smaragd weight from the same terraces.

others.name: Unendlich
others.note: A selection made only in years the house judges fit, a Riesling from 1998 and a Grüner Veltliner from 2003; the name means endless.

traps: F.X. Pichler is not Rudi Pichler or Pichler-Krutzler: several unrelated Pichler estates work the Wachau, so read the initials.
Smaragd is a trademark of the Vinea Wachau, a growers' association: it measures ripeness, says nothing of the vineyard and has no standing in Austrian law.

cards.front: F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg: what rock lies under its terraces?
cards.back: Gföhl gneiss, a metamorphic rock, with patches of loess that the Ice Ages left on the sheltered south east slope.

cards.front: Where does the name of F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg come from, and how old is it?
cards.back: From the baroque Kellerschlössl of Dürnstein; the name dates only from 1787 and gathered several smaller vineyards.

questions.q: Smaragd on the label of F.X. Pichler's Riesling Ried Kellerberg leads a guest to expect sweetness. What is true of the wine?
opts: It is dry: the word marks the Wachau's ripest dry style
It is late picked and keeps some natural sugar
It is a sweet wine of grapes touched by noble rot
It is a dry wine aged a year in new oak
questions.exp: Smaragd is the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, fermented dry to at least twelve and a half per cent alcohol; the codex allows it no hint of oak, so the new oak answer is wrong as well.

questions.q: By the house's own account, the Riesling Kellerberg of which vintage first carried the name of F.X. Pichler abroad?
questions.exp: The house dates its breakthrough abroad to the Kellerberg of 1990; 1983 is the founding of the Vinea Wachau, 1985 Austria's wine scandal and 2009 the house's new winery.

wine.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Singerriedel at Spitz, first recorded in 1486, narrow terraces held by dry stone walls: shallow, sandy, meagre soil over paragneiss, with mica schist and bands of quartzite lower down; Riesling grows on the steep terraces and Grüner Veltliner at the foot.
wine.making: The terraces are harvested by hand late in the autumn, as the Wachau DAC requires and a Smaragd's ripeness asks, and the Vinea Wachau's codex allows no enrichment. Fermented dry in stainless steel, the wine is often then raised in large wooden casks of three to five thousand litres, which give it no taste of oak; some vintages stay in steel.
wine.glass: Apricot, ripe yellow peach and lime zest, with orange blossom, over the smoky note of wet rock; full and creamy yet dry, with firm acidity and a long trail of salt.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it settles after about five years and, in a strong vintage, goes on for two decades and more, gaining honey and dried apricot.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; if a young bottle seems tight, give it an hour in a decanter; a generous white wine glass.

label.means: The ripest of the Vinea Wachau's three dry styles, from twelve and a half per cent alcohol, named after the emerald green lizard.
The single vineyard, a steep wall of narrow terraces at Spitz, first recorded in 1486.
The valley's appellation from the 2020 vintage, which demands that every wine be picked by hand.

records.table: Narrow dry stone terraces at Spitz, in the western Wachau, are home to Franz Hirtzberger's Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel. Full and creamy yet dry, with ripe peach and apricot on a stony core, it is worth a decade in the cellar.
records.story: The modern Hirtzberger estate, at Spitz in the western Wachau, begins with the grower of the family who took over his parents' holding in 1948: by the account of the Vinea Wachau, he bottled its wine for the first time and picked out the terraces of single vineyards the family farms. In 1983 he was one of the growers who founded the Vinea Wachau. His son took over the estate that same year, saw it through the wine scandal of 1985 and led the association from 1988 to 2012, as the dry wines of the Wachau found their way abroad. The Singerriedel, the steep wall of narrow terraces on paragneiss at Spitz, gave the house its signature Riesling, picked late for Smaragd and fermented dry. From the 2020 vintage the Wachau DAC has carried it as a Ried, a single vineyard of its own. In 2014 a son of the family founded a separate estate, the Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, so read the whole name on the label: the Singerriedel of Spitz is Franz Hirtzberger's.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Honivogl
others.note: Grüner Veltliner of full Smaragd weight, ripe, powerful and dry, often named with the house beside the Singerriedel.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Hochrain
others.note: A second single vineyard Riesling Smaragd of the house, from the Hochrain.

traps: The Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, founded in 2014 by a son of the family, is a separate estate; Franz Hirtzberger is the house at Spitz.
Honivogl and Singerriedel are vineyard names, not producers.
However ripe it is, a Smaragd is a dry wine: the word measures ripeness, never sweetness.

cards.front: On what rock and soil does Franz Hirtzberger's Singerriedel stand?
cards.back: Paragneiss, with mica schist and bands of quartzite, under shallow, sandy soil held by dry stone walls.

cards.front: What did the Hirtzberger grower who took over in 1948 do, by the Vinea Wachau's account?

questions.q: Where do the vines of Franz Hirtzberger's Riesling Smaragd Ried Singerriedel grow?

The deep loess plain east of Krems
The sandstone hill above Zöbing
A fan of stream debris at Unterloiben

report: Founded is left empty: one account has the family buying its first vines at Spitz in the late nineteenth century and another speaks of a farm of the thirteenth century; no house page was found to settle it.

The grower of 1948 (born 1923, died 2007, by the Vinea Wachau's own notice) is described rather than named, as his dates rest on that one source; his son and grandson are living and are not named, and the brother who founded the Weinhofmeisterei in 2014 should be added to people.json by the read together agent (Mathias Hirtzberger).

The grower of 1948 as a founder of the Vinea Wachau in 1983 rests on the association's own notice and its fortieth anniversary release, which lists him among the founding fathers (the Sommelier Academy agrees); his first bottling is on the house's profile there, with no year given; the son's leadership from 1988 to 2012 rests on the Vinea Wachau's own notice, with Decanter calling him its long standing president.

The making rests on Falstaff's entries for several vintages (steel tank and large wooden barrel) and a merchant's listing that gives casks of three to five thousand litres; Falstaff lists steel alone for one vintage, so the record says most vintages.
The Ried Hochrain Riesling Smaragd is attested by Falstaff and a second listing only as a wine, so its note says nothing of the site.
The table and the ageing keep the library's view of a ripe, long lived Riesling; the region line's 'richest, most honeyed' is a judgement and is not repeated.

changed: wine.sites, the Ried label line, table, story and the wine question: the Singerriedel is at Spitz, no longer at the entrance to Spitz or the edge of the village, which no source of this check gave; the Vinea Wachau's sheet gives its first record, 1486, which the sites and the label now carry.

wine.making: the wine is often raised in large wooden casks of three to five thousand litres after its steel fermentation, and some vintages stay in steel, in place of most vintages in casks of several thousand litres; one merchant gives the casks and their size, another a recent vintage in steel alone.

questions[1].exp: the Traditionsweingüter is a separate, private association, no longer the Kamptal and Kremstal association, since its members reach into the Traisental, the Wagram, Vienna and Carnuntum.
open: The first bottling and the choice of single vineyards rest on the Vinea Wachau's profile of the house, which credits them to the eldest Franz without a year; the record keeps the Vinea's word for it.
The vessels change by vintage, steel alone in one merchant's recent sheet and steel then large wood in another's; the record says often.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt
wine.classification: Smaragd of the Vinea Wachau; Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Wachau DAC
wine.sites: The Schütt, astride the boundary of Dürnstein and Unterloiben, on a fan of stream debris at the mouth of the Menthalgraben, between the Höhereck and the Loibenberg: deep, sandy and stony soil of weathered gneiss, poor in fine earth, so it drains fast.
wine.making: The grapes come in by hand, as the Wachau DAC requires, late in the autumn, and the Vinea Wachau's codex rules out any enrichment. Once fermented dry, the wine is raised mostly in large, old oak casks that give it air and texture rather than a taste of wood, with some stainless steel beside them.
wine.glass: White pepper, green pear and quince over lentils and wet stone, with tobacco leaf as it ages; dense and savoury rather than fruity, dry and long, with a fine, stony grip.
wine.ageing: Dense and savoury young, it deepens over five to ten years, and a strong year will hold for twenty years or longer.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; give a young bottle an hour of air in a decanter; a large bowled white wine glass.

label.means: Emerald, for the green lizard: the Vinea Wachau's ripest dry style, at twelve and a half per cent alcohol or more.
The single vineyard, a fan of gneiss debris between Dürnstein and Unterloiben.
The baroque image of the saint that has marked Knoll bottles since 1962.

records.table: The baroque Saint Urban stands on the label of Emmerich Knoll's Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt, grown on a stony fan of gneiss at Unterloiben. Peppery, savoury and dense, it is long lived: cellar it for years and give it some air in the glass.
records.story: Since the early nineteenth century the Knolls have grown vines at Unterloiben, at the eastern end of the Wachau. In the house's memory, Knoll wine went into glass bottles from the 1950s, and in 1962 the baroque image of Saint Urban first appeared on the label, where it has stayed. The Knoll wines carry the styles of the Vinea Wachau, the valley's growers' association of 1983, in which Smaragd marks the ripest dry wine. When the scandal of 1985 brought a tighter wine law, the house kept its own pace, with late picking and large old oak casks. From 1988 it added a Vinothekfüllung, a dry selection of late picked Grüner Veltliner made in nearly every year, joined by a Riesling in 2000. Its vineyards lie around the village, the Loibenberg, the Kellerberg and the Kreutles among them, with the Pfaffenberg across the border in the Kremstal, yet the house names the Schütt before them all. With the 2020 vintage the Schütt became a Ried of the Wachau DAC. Grüner Veltliner from the Wachau can last for decades, and the Schütt is the bottle that shows it.

others.name: Riesling Smaragd Ried Schütt
others.note: Riesling from the same stony fan, slow to open and long lived.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Vinothekfüllung

others.name: Riesling Ried Pfaffenberg
others.note: From a site across the border in the Kremstal, so it carries no Smaragd.

Vinothekfüllung is Knoll's own word for a selection; neither the law nor the Vinea Wachau defines it.
The Saint Urban figure on the label is the house's own mark, not a regional seal.

cards.front: What did Emmerich Knoll add to its range in 1988?

questions.q: Emmerich Knoll raises its Grüner Veltliner Smaragd Ried Schütt in oak, yet it shows no taste of wood. Why?
opts: The casks are large and old, so they give no oak flavour
It spends only a few days in new barrels
The barrels are charred heavily to hide their flavour
It is aged in chestnut casks, never in oak
questions.exp: Knoll raises its Smaragd mostly in large old oak casks, with some steel, which give air and texture without wood flavour; a few days in new barrels would leave toast and vanilla, and the codex allows a Smaragd no hint of oak.

The large old oak casks with some steel rest on an importer's sheet (The Source Imports) and the Sommelier Academy; the sizes, the overnight settling and the avoided malolactic fermentation rest on the importer alone and are left out.

wine.name: Riesling Zöbinger Heiligenstein Alte Reben
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines, a few of them planted before the Second World War.
wine.sites: The Zöbinger Heiligenstein above Zöbing, a bare hill of Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, its face held by dry stone terraces built by hand from the 1920s; part of the house's share is trained on the Lyra, a divided, lyre shaped trellis.
wine.making: The juice ferments in stainless steel at fifteen to twenty degrees Celsius, and the wine then rests on its lees, in steel and in large wooden casks, until it is bottled some months later.
wine.glass: Orange peel, yellow peach and apricot over smoke, warm stone and dried thyme; dry and firm, with fine, salty acidity, a silky weight and real length.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after five to seven years, and a strong vintage outlives two decades.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter while it is young; a white wine glass with room in the bowl.

label.means: The single vineyard on the sandstone hill above Zöbing; newer labels print Ried Heiligenstein.
Old vines: the house's old plantings on the Heiligenstein.
The Traditionsweingüter's own mark for a site it ranks Erste Lage; Austrian law framed classified sites only in 2023.
The appellation since the 2008 vintage, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all.

records.table: Old vines on the Zöbinger Heiligenstein, the Kamptal's hill of desert sandstone above Zöbing, are the source of Bründlmayer's Riesling Alte Reben. Dry and firm, apricot and orange peel over smoke and warm stone, it keeps for decades.
records.story: Bründlmayer is a family estate of Langenlois, in the Kamptal, whose Heuriger stands in a Renaissance vintner's house in the town. Its signature hill, the Heiligenstein above Zöbing, is usually said to appear in a monastic register of 1280 as Hellenstein, for the heat of its bare slope, before the name became Heiligenstein, the holy stone. From the 1920s dry stone terraces were built by hand on its face, and some of the vines on it lived through the Second World War. In 1980 the son of the house succeeded his parents; in time part of the hill was trained on the Lyra trellis, and a sparkling wine made in the bottle joined the range. In 1996 the Bründlmayers lent a hand when a new family took on Schloss Gobelsburg nearby. The Kamptal DAC followed with the 2008 vintage, and from 2010 the Traditionsweingüter, a private association of estates, ranked its members' sites, the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2015 the vineyards were certified organic. Alte Reben is the house's selection from its old vines on the hill, Austrian Riesling grown on desert sandstone rather than on the Wachau's gneiss.

others.name: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm
others.note: Grüner Veltliner from deep loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, rich and long.

others.name: Riesling Ried Heiligenstein
others.note: The hill's Riesling without the old vine selection, the step below the Alte Reben.

others.name: Extra Brut Reserve
others.note: Sparkling wine made by the traditional method, its second fermentation in the bottle.

traps: The Heiligenstein is Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, not limestone, whatever its holy stone name suggests.
The Kamptal is not the Wachau: Smaragd, Federspiel and Steinfeder never appear on Bründlmayer's labels.
1ÖTW is the private mark of the Traditionsweingüter, not a rank in Austrian wine law.

cards.front: Bründlmayer's Heiligenstein: what rock is the hill, despite its holy name?
cards.back: Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic grains, laid down in a desert; no limestone.

cards.front: What does Alte Reben on Bründlmayer's Heiligenstein Riesling mean?

questions.q: By the house's own sheets, how is Bründlmayer's Riesling Alte Reben from the Heiligenstein made?

Fermented and aged a year in new barriques
Left sweet by stopping the fermentation early
Picked frozen on the vine in a hard winter
questions.exp: By the house's own sheets the juice ferments in stainless steel and the wine then rests on its lees in steel and large wooden casks; a year in new barriques would give it toast and vanilla.

report: Founded is left empty: one lexicon dates the family's tradition to 1581, but the house's own pages read here gave no year, so the story does not use it.
The register of 1280 and the name Hellenstein rest on the wein.plus lexicon and a wine wiki, both read through search summaries, and are told as what is usually said.

The making rests on the house's own factsheets: steel at fifteen to twenty degrees and lees until bottling in the summer for 2018, steel then a wooden cask of 2,500 litres for 2023 (bottled in February 2024); the record says many vintages and the year after the harvest.

The terraces of the 1920s, the vines that lived through the war, fertiliser given up in 1979, the Lyra and the organic certificate of 2015 are the house's own account; the son who took over around 1980 is living and is not named.
The Kamptal DAC of 2008 and the ÖTW ranking from 2010 are the library's; Austrian Wine confirms that 1ÖTW is a private classification outside the wine law.
The library names the sparkling wine Brut Reserve; the house's shop lists an Extra Brut Reserve, so the record uses that name.
Two of the house's Heiligenstein sheets disagree on vessels (2024 steel alone for the Riesling without the old vine selection, 2018 partly big casks), so the others line says nothing of the cellar.

wine.name: Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the Kamptal DAC; Erste Lage, marked 1ÖTW, of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter
wine.sites: The Lamm, on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, where the hill eases into gentler slopes: deep loess and loam, mixed with material washed down from the hill's Permian rock and volcanic stone.
wine.making: Fermented and matured in large traditional casks of five to six thousand litres, made of Austrian oak from the nearby Manhartsberg forest, with an occasional new cask among them. Under the Kamptal DAC a single vineyard wine may not be submitted for its state test number before April of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and yellow apple over white pepper, lentils and toasted hazelnut, with a hint of honey; broad, creamy and dry, fresh in its acidity and savoury to the last.
wine.ageing: Its richness makes it ready on release; it builds depth over five to ten years, and a strong vintage keeps fifteen years or longer.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; a young bottle wants half an hour in a decanter; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard of loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein.
An Erste Lage in the private ranking of the Traditionsweingüter; classified sites entered Austrian law only in 2023.
Grüner Veltliner and Riesling above all: the appellation of the Kamptal since the 2008 vintage.

records.table: Deep loess and loam on the south east side of the Heiligenstein, a hill where the monks of Zwettl held vines from 1171, as the house tells it, carry Schloss Gobelsburg's Grüner Veltliner Ried Lamm. Broad and dry, pear, quince and white pepper, it matures in large Austrian oak casks.
records.story: The Cistercian monks of Zwettl Abbey received their first vineyards in the Kamptal, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg, in 1171, by the house's history. The castle of Gobelsburg passed through many noble families until 1740, when its last aristocratic owner sold it to the abbey, which already held an estate at Kammern nearby; late in the eighteenth century, after a fire at Kammern, the making of the wine moved to Gobelsburg. The monks ran the cellar themselves until 1995. In 1996 a family took over the running of the estate on a long lease, with early help from the Bründlmayers of Langenlois, while the abbey kept the ownership. The new managers added a Tradition line, an ode to the cellar ways of Gobelsburg between 1800 and 1850. The Lamm, with the Heiligenstein, came to be counted an Erste Lage in the private ranking of the Traditionsweingüter, and the Kamptal became a DAC with the 2008 vintage. In 2021 the house marked eight hundred and fifty years of winegrowing. Fullest of its Grüner Veltliners, the Lamm is a Kamptal wine of full weight from loess and loam that carries a monastic estate's history.

report: Founded is the library's 1171, but by the house's own history 1171 is the year the monks of Zwettl received their first Kamptal vineyards, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg; the abbey bought the castle in 1740, so the plan's 'estate at Gobelsburg recorded from 1171' is loose.

The library's trap says the estate is run under lease by its winemaker; the house speaks of management by a family from 1996 with the abbey as owner, and no source read here gives a lease, so the record says the running of the estate.

The region's producers line has the Tradition wines made in old wooden casks moved on wheels, and the library has racking by the moon; neither was confirmed by any source read here, so the record says only an ode to the cellar ways of 1800 to 1850 (the house and Skurnik).
The casks of five thousand litres and more, a few new, rest on two importer notes for the 2019 and 2022 vintages; the Manhartsberg oak on the house's page and an importer.
The family that took over in 1996 and the couple of Bründlmayer who helped them are living and are not named.
The eight hundred and fiftieth year in 2021 rests on the house's jubilee edition and a wine travel page (Wine in Time).
